newsitem.title: INDIA: India moves towards realistic power tariffs.
newsitem.headline: India moves towards realistic power tariffs.

text.p: India is moving towards realistic power sector tariffs to ensure economic viability and meet a huge shortfall after incentives failed to impress foreign investors, officials and analysts said on Thursday.

The government's offer of fast approvals, a five-year tax holiday and a 16 percent return on equity have not produced dramatic investments that India looked for when it launched an economic reform programme in 1991.
"The whole cost structure has to change," Anushree Sinha, economist at the National Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER), told Reuters.

Power Minister Y.K. Alagh told a committee of lawmakers on Wednesday that the government would announce a new power policy after the monsoon session of Parliament, which is scheduled to start in the third week of July.
The policy will encompass all aspects of the power sector, including generation, transmission and distribution.
The Financial Express on Thursday quoted Alagh as saying the government would pass in the monsoon session a law to enable a new tariff structure for electricity, which in India is heavily subsidised.
"Private investment will be available only if they are able to get a return for their investment. They have to be assured of at least 16 percent return," Alagh said.
During the Eighth Plan (1992-97), India could create fresh capacity for only 17,700 megawatts against a targeted 30,538 MW. The shortfall is mainly attributed to flagging investment.
Only three foreign investment projects, involving less than 45 billion rupees ($1.25 billion), have got off the ground.
In the 11 months to February of the year 1996/97, growth in electricity generation slumped to 3.6 percent, compared with 8.3 percent for the same period of 1995/96.

Two years ago, the government estimated India needed nearly $80 billion to overcome supply gaps. With the country aiming for a sustained 7.0 percent growth over the Ninth Plan (1997-2002), demand for power is soaring.
Economists say state-run electricity boards have been pushed towards financial bankruptcy by subsidies aimed at pleasing a politically powerful farm lobby.
"Agricultural landlords get the benefit. Subsidies are politically targeted, not socially targeted," Sinha said.

After it ended a state power monopoly in 1991, India's federal government initially offered "counter-guarantees" to eight private power projects in order to assure payments on behalf of financially weak state electricity boards (SEBs).
But it stopped the practice amid howls of protest from opposition parties and a frowning World Bank, which said it was not a government's job to bear private investment risks.

India also gave up negotiated power projects in favour of open competitive bidding after a painful series of environomental and political protests over a $2.3 billion project being built by the united States' Enron Corp.
The Enron project's terms were altered by a new state government in the western province of Maharashtra.
Alagh was quoted as saying the government was working out an alternative to counter-guarantees.

Last December, state chief ministers agreed to set up state-level power regulators who would fix tariffs, and encourage private participation in the distribution of electricity now carried out by ailing state companies.
In 1996/97 (April-March), commercial losses of the state power sector amounted to 104.9 billion rupees ($2.93 billion), up from 83.24 billion rupees ($2.32 billion) in 1995/96. ($1=35.8 rupees).
